title: Helio Bank - Procurement/Legal/Security Exhibit: Audit logs + retention
summary: Helio Bank legal/procurement requested specific Security Exhibit language covering audit log availability, retention, and export (SIEM). Redwood clarified current controls (schema v1, event_id for dedupe, export targets, redaction), distinguished Hosted/Dedicated vs Private retention responsibilities, and avoided committing to hard guarantees beyond current SLA/SLO posture. Agreed Redwood will propose contract language focused on audit log capability + customer-controlled retention for Private, and provide written guidance for deduplication and retention options.
next_steps: Redwood (Michael Grant) to send proposed Security Exhibit clause language for audit logging (Hosted/Dedicated vs Private) by 2026-02-10
Redwood (Naomi Feldman) to share externally-safe audit logging FAQ wording + schema v1 field overview by 2026-02-10
Redwood (Kevin Osei) to share SIEM export guidance (Splunk HEC + Azure Sentinel) and de-dupe recommendations using event_id by 2026-02-12
Helio Bank (John Patel) to mark up the proposed clause and flag any regulatory wording requirements (FFIEC/retention) by 2026-02-14
Schedule follow-up 30 min to close redlines on Security Exhibit (Liam to coordinate)
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: Helio Bank - Procurement/Legal/Security Exhibit: Audit logs + retention
Date: 2026-02-06
Time: 3:00pm - 3:46pm PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Liam O'Rourke (Redwood Inference)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference)
- Michael Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference)
- Sarah Kim (Helio Bank)
- John Patel (Helio Bank)
- Dana Ruiz (Helio Bank)
- Priya Desai (Helio Bank)

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, cool. I think we’re all here. Sarah, John, Dana, Priya—thanks for making time. This is the procurement / legal security exhibit review, specifically audit logs and retention language. Michael from our privacy and legal side is here, Naomi who owns security & compliance on product, Markus SE, and Kevin who owns the export pipeline.

[00:18] Sarah Kim: Thanks Liam. Yeah, we want to make sure the exhibit matches what we need for regulated workloads. We have a couple clauses we need to add around audit logging, retention period, and—frankly—what happens if the logs aren’t available.

[00:34] John Patel: And to be explicit, we’re not trying to rewrite your product roadmap, but we need commitments in the contract: audit logs for admin actions, retention minimums, and access/export rights.

[00:46] Dana Ruiz: Plus, we had an incident last year with another vendor where “audit logs” meant like, a CSV of some UI actions. We need something SIEM-consumable, consistent schema, and a way to correlate actions to identities.

[01:03] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. Maybe we start with what you’re asking for in the exhibit and then we can map to what we do today, and what we can put in writing without overpromising.

[01:14] John Patel: Sure. Our proposed language is basically:
1) Provider will maintain audit logs for all administrative and security relevant actions.
2) Provider will retain audit logs for 12 months.
3) Provider will provide audit logs to Customer upon request and/or via export.
4) Provider will ensure audit logs are immutable and cannot be altered by Provider personnel without leaving evidence.

[01:40] Michael Grant: Thanks. Helpful. I’ll flag up front: we can usually commit to capabilities and process controls, but absolute terms like “all actions” and “immutable” can be tricky, especially across Hosted versus Private. But let’s unpack each.

[01:55] Naomi Feldman: On “administrative and security relevant actions,” we’re standardizing a sensitive-actions taxonomy across the platform. So not “every button click,” but all the things you’d expect: RBAC changes, API key lifecycle, policy changes, retention/residency settings, export config changes, Private install/upgrade/rollback.

[02:14] Dana Ruiz: That’s good. We’d want specifically: role changes, key creation/rotation/revocation, SSO config changes, and any policy or routing changes that can change data exposure.

[02:27] Markus Klein: Yes. Those map directly to our event types. We’ve got a canonical schema—versioned. Each event has actor identity, action type, target resource, timestamps, and correlation IDs.

[02:40] Priya Desai: Correlation IDs meaning like request ID and trace ID?

[02:44] Markus Klein: Exactly. request_id and trace_id, and for admin workflows we also include an admin_action_id when it spans multiple calls. (Sometimes transcription calls it “admin auction id,” sorry.)

[03:00] Kevin Osei: And the event has an event_id which is globally unique for dedupe. Because delivery is at-least-once in parts of the pipeline.

[03:10] John Patel: Okay. The contract language though: “retain 12 months.” Can you do that today?

[03:18] Liam O'Rourke: It depends on deployment mode. For Private deployment—where you run it in your VPC or on-prem—you control retention because the logs are in your environment and you can ship them to Splunk or Sentinel or whatever. For Hosted/Dedicated, we have a standard retention window and an add-on for extended retention.

[03:38] Sarah Kim: What’s the standard window?

[03:40] Naomi Feldman: Today, standard is 90 days for Hosted audit log retention in the platform. For some enterprise tiers we can extend—contractually and technically—via add-on. But I want to be careful: exact numbers might vary by region and tier, and we should confirm what we can offer you specifically.

[04:02] John Patel: For us, 12 months is kind of non-negotiable for regulated audit trails.

[04:07] Dana Ruiz: Especially if we have to do investigations that are long running.

[04:12] Kevin Osei: For Hosted, our strongest recommendation is to export to your SIEM and retain there for 12 months (or longer). We support streaming export so you’re not limited by our UI retention. That’s usually how banks handle it with SaaS providers.

[04:28] Priya Desai: But if export fails for some time, then you lose data.

[04:33] Kevin Osei: Right, and that’s where we talk about buffering and retry. In Hosted, our exporter supports batching, backoff, and we expose metrics for delivery latency and drop rate. In Private, you can also configure local buffering. But no system can guarantee zero loss under all conditions; what we can do is define delivery semantics and controls.

[04:55] Michael Grant: From a contract standpoint, we can propose language like: “Provider will make audit log events available for export and will retain them for a minimum period in the service; Customer is responsible for long-term retention after export.” That’s a common split.

[05:12] John Patel: We still need a minimum retention in the service itself. 90 days might be okay if export is truly supported and documented, but we also need some assurance that it’s part of the product, not best-effort.

[05:26] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. We can include in the exhibit that audit log export is an enterprise feature, supported for the term, with documented formats and authentication.

[05:36] Dana Ruiz: And coverage: you said “sensitive action taxonomy.” Can we get a list? Like, what actions are guaranteed to be logged.

[05:44] Naomi Feldman: Yes—we can share the externally-safe list of event categories and examples, plus the schema field definitions. We’re moving to 100% coverage for that sensitive list. Some of that is already shipping; some is being completed. We can be clear on what is available in your intended deployment mode at signature and what is on our near-term plan.

[06:06] John Patel: We need to avoid “roadmap” language. If it’s not available at signature, we can’t treat it as a contractual obligation.

[06:13] Michael Grant: That’s fair. We can write the clause to reflect “as generally available in the Services” and attach a description of current audit logging features. For anything not GA, we shouldn’t commit.

[06:28] Sarah Kim: Can we talk about “immutable”? We have a template clause that says logs must be tamper-evident.

[06:36] Kevin Osei: In Hosted, the events go into a centralized append-only store with access controls and audit on access. Internally, we restrict who can access raw logs and any access itself is logged. In Private, you can route events to your immutability controls—WORM storage, immutable S3 buckets, etc.

[06:56] Dana Ruiz: Does Redwood staff have the ability to delete audit logs?

[07:01] Naomi Feldman: In Hosted, we have retention policies, so data ages out per retention. We do not have a “delete this customer’s audit logs” button in the console. Any support-led data handling is controlled and logged. For Private, you control your environment.

[07:18] Michael Grant: If you’re asking for “provider cannot alter logs,” we can commit to access control, separation of duties, and logging of administrative access. Absolute impossibility is hard to prove contractually; we usually commit to tamper-evident controls and policies.

[07:37] John Patel: Ok. Another thing: the definition of “audit logs.” We need to be clear it includes API actions, not just UI.

[07:45] Markus Klein: Yep. We emit audit events from API gateway and control plane services. UI actions in the Console ultimately call those APIs, so they’re covered. We capture actor identity consistently.

[07:58] Priya Desai: Identity meaning the user who clicked, not some service account.

[08:02] Markus Klein: Correct. For UI, the actor is the authenticated human identity. For automated actions (like a CI pipeline using an API key), the actor is the credential identity; we also include the principal type. And if there’s impersonation (support), we include both the acting admin and the impersonated user.

[08:25] Dana Ruiz: Source IP captured?

[08:27] Markus Klein: Yes for gateway events, source IP is captured and normalized. For private deployments behind proxies, it depends on headers and your ingress config, but we document that.

[08:41] Sarah Kim: Can we just go down the list and see what you can accept in the clause?

[08:45] Liam O'Rourke: Sure. John, your clause #1: “all administrative and security relevant actions.” Naomi, can we scope that to “all sensitive actions as defined by Redwood and provided to Customer”?

[08:57] Naomi Feldman: That’s exactly how we phrase it internally: “sensitive actions taxonomy.” And we can attach the taxonomy categories to the exhibit.

[09:07] John Patel: We’d want the taxonomy attachment to be part of the contract, not a link that can change.

[09:13] Michael Grant: We can attach a PDF or snapshot as an exhibit attachment. We’ll mark it as informational describing current coverage; we can also include a statement that we won’t materially reduce audit logging capabilities without notice.

[09:30] Dana Ruiz: “Materially reduce” is vague.

[09:33] Michael Grant: True. We can propose something like: “Provider will not disable audit logging for the covered actions.” But again, there are edge cases, like service outages.

[09:44] Kevin Osei: And we should discuss delivery guarantees. During an outage, services shouldn’t block admin actions because audit sink is down. So events can buffer and flush later. That can mean delayed delivery.

[09:58] Priya Desai: That’s fine. We can accept delayed, but we need eventual delivery and an alert if the pipeline is behind.

[10:07] Kevin Osei: We have SLOs we’re implementing: delivery latency and drop rate. We can share the targets and our operational runbook approach, but it’s not typically in the contract.

[10:20] John Patel: Okay. Clause #2: “retain 12 months.” You said Hosted is 90 days standard.

[10:27] Liam O'Rourke: Right. For Private, you can do 12 months easily since you retain in your SIEM or storage. For Hosted, we can either (a) add extended retention or (b) write contract to say you will export to your SIEM for long-term retention.

[10:44] Sarah Kim: If we choose Private, then retention is on us, but we still need the product to be capable of exporting reliably.

[10:52] Markus Klein: Yes. Export supports Splunk HEC and Azure Sentinel/Log Analytics. Also generic HTTPS target. For authentication, we support tokens, basic, and mTLS depending on destination.

[11:08] Dana Ruiz: Does export include the full event? Or does it truncate?

[11:12] Kevin Osei: Full event as per schema. But we intentionally do not log secrets or raw payloads. So you won’t see prompt content or API key material. You’ll see hashes/redacted forms for sensitive identifiers.

[11:27] Dana Ruiz: Good. We don’t want PII in logs, but we need enough to investigate.

[11:34] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. Actor, action, target resource IDs, before/after summaries for config changes—without dumping entire configs.

[11:46] John Patel: Clause #3: “provide audit logs upon request.” If we do Private, that’s our responsibility. For Hosted, can you provide exports on request?

[11:55] Liam O'Rourke: We can provide access via API and export configuration. Support can also assist, but we’d prefer self-serve export. In contract, we can say we provide mechanisms to access and export.

[12:10] Sarah Kim: Clause #4: immutability. We can adjust to “tamper-evident.”

[12:14] Michael Grant: That’s more workable. We can say: “Provider maintains access controls and logging such that modifications are restricted and any administrative access is logged.” And for Private: “Customer may implement immutability controls in their environment.”

[12:33] Dana Ruiz: We need to ensure Redwood personnel access is limited and audited.

[12:38] Michael Grant: Yes, that’s SOC 2 aligned. We can reference our controls. We don’t usually incorporate SOC2 reports in the contract, but we can provide them under NDA.

[12:50] John Patel: We’ve already requested the SOC2 report. Separate thread.

[12:54] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, we’ll follow up on that.

[13:00] Priya Desai: Quick technical question: duplicates. You mentioned at-least-once delivery. If our SIEM sees duplicates, what do we do?

[13:08] Kevin Osei: Great question. We include event_id. You dedupe on that. Some customers also dedupe on (event_id, tenant_id). We’ll provide recommended queries for Splunk and Sentinel.

[13:22] Dana Ruiz: And ordering? We might see events out of order.

[13:25] Kevin Osei: Yes, possible. Each has occurred_at timestamp and received_at. Use occurred_at for sequence, but expect slight skew.

[13:35] John Patel: Contractually, I don’t want to commit to exact ordering anyway. But we do want reliability language.

[13:42] Michael Grant: We can add a clause that audit logs are provided “on an at-least-once basis” and may include duplicates, and the event_id supports de-duplication. That’s transparent and defensible.

[13:56] Sarah Kim: That’s actually good to put in writing. We’ve had issues where vendors pretend duplicates are a bug.

[14:03] Liam O'Rourke: Makes sense.

[14:06] Dana Ruiz: Another point: do the logs include changes to export configuration itself? Like if someone points exports to a different endpoint.

[14:15] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Export destination changes are sensitive actions and are audited with before/after summary.

[14:23] Priya Desai: In Private deployments, who is the “actor” for installer actions? Sometimes it’s just someone on a bastion.

[14:31] Markus Klein: In Private, installer emits events with operator identity when available—like if you authenticate via your SSO or provide an operator identifier. Worst case it can be “unknown operator” plus source host info. We’re improving that, but we don’t want to claim perfect attribution if the environment doesn’t provide identity.

[14:54] Dana Ruiz: Ok. We can accept “best available identity” with documentation.

[15:00] John Patel: Switching to retention again: if we do Hosted, can you offer 12 months retention in-product?

[15:07] Liam O'Rourke: Potentially via an add-on, but I need to confirm packaging and pricing with our team. For many customers, exporting is preferred. But we can come back with an option.

[15:21] Sarah Kim: We don’t want a surprise cost late.

[15:24] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. I’ll take that as an action item: we’ll confirm what we can offer for extended retention, and what’s included.

[15:34] Dana Ruiz: Data residency: for Hosted, where are audit logs stored?

[15:40] Naomi Feldman: Same region as the tenant’s configured residency, subject to our region support. For Private, you control. For Hosted multi-region, we keep control plane and logs aligned to your configured region, and exports go to your SIEM endpoint.

[15:59] Priya Desai: If your exporter is sending out of region, that could be an issue.

[16:04] Kevin Osei: The exporter sends to whatever endpoint you configure. We can document recommended patterns, and you can choose in-region SIEM collectors.

[16:14] John Patel: Okay. Let’s talk about what you can put in writing without referencing internal docs that change.

[16:21] Michael Grant: Here’s what I propose we do: we draft an “Audit Logging” section in the Security Exhibit with:
- Definition of audit logs
- Covered actions (by category)
- Fields included (high-level)
- Retention (Hosted minimum + customer export responsibility)
- Export support (supported targets)
- Delivery semantics (at-least-once, dedupe with event_id)
- Access controls / tamper-evident statement

[16:51] John Patel: That’s good.

[16:53] Sarah Kim: And we still want a retention number.

[16:56] Liam O'Rourke: For Hosted, we can commit to a minimum retention in the service, e.g., “not less than 90 days,” and then include “export available for long-term retention.” If we can offer 12 months as an add-on, we’ll present it as an option.

[17:16] Dana Ruiz: Make sure the clause doesn’t say logs are the only source of truth. We’ll treat them as an investigative tool.

[17:23] Naomi Feldman: Yes, that’s consistent. Also we should state what’s intentionally excluded for privacy and security—no secrets, no raw prompts.

[17:35] Priya Desai: If you don’t log prompts, how do we investigate misuse?

[17:40] Markus Klein: We log the action and context—like “API key used from IP X to call model Y”—but not the content. Most banks prefer that. If you need content-level logging, you typically do that on your side at the application layer.

[17:58] Dana Ruiz: That aligns with our internal policies.

[18:02] John Patel: Competitor comparison: we’ve seen OpenAI and Anthropic provide some audit logs but it’s limited, and AWS Bedrock is more like CloudTrail. We want to make sure Redwood isn’t weaker.

[18:14] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. We can’t speak for them in contract, but our posture is that enterprise customers need SOC2-style auditability, and we’re building to that.

[18:25] Sarah Kim: Ok.

[18:27] (crosstalk)

[18:29] Dana Ruiz: One more: access to audit logs. Is it restricted by RBAC? Like only auditors can view.

[18:36] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Audit log viewing/export configuration is permissioned. And changes to those permissions are themselves audited.

[18:47] John Patel: Great.

[18:49] Sarah Kim: What about subcontractors? If you use sub-processors for logging.

[18:55] Michael Grant: We have a list of subprocessors for the service; for Private, you’d run in your environment, so fewer. For Hosted, the logging pipeline uses our cloud infrastructure providers. We can point you to the subprocessor list and DPA.

[19:12] John Patel: Ok.

[19:13] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we’re aligned on substance. The open items are: (1) can we offer extended retention to 12 months in Hosted as an add-on; (2) draft the precise clause language.

[19:26] Sarah Kim: Plus we want the attachment describing event categories.

[19:29] Naomi Feldman: I’ll provide a safe-to-share summary of the sensitive actions categories and example event types, not internal ticket references.

[19:38] Kevin Osei: And I’ll include de-dupe guidance and exporter targets. We’ve got Splunk HEC and Azure Sentinel. If you’re on something else, we can discuss.

[19:49] Priya Desai: We’re primarily Splunk today.

[19:51] Kevin Osei: Great. We can share sample HEC config and recommended fields mapping.

[19:58] John Patel: We’ll need the “at-least-once” language and duplicates clearly described.

[20:05] Michael Grant: Yes. We’ll draft it so it doesn’t sound like a defect, but a known delivery property.

[20:12] Dana Ruiz: Also can you include that logs have timestamps in UTC and include tenant and project scope.

[20:19] Markus Klein: Yes. tenant_id and project_id are included when applicable. Time is ISO 8601, UTC.

[20:28] Sarah Kim: Ok.

[20:30] Liam O'Rourke: We have about 25 minutes left. Do you want to walk through redlines live, or should we send proposed language first?

[20:38] John Patel: Send proposed language first. Live redlines without a document is inefficient.

[20:42] Liam O'Rourke: Agreed.

[20:45] Dana Ruiz: One last check: if Redwood has an outage, will admin actions fail because you can’t write the audit log?

[20:53] Kevin Osei: No, we don’t hard-block. We buffer. Worst case, if the buffer is full, we have backpressure policies, but we try to avoid customer-impacting blocks. We’ll document failure modes.

[21:10] Dana Ruiz: Okay. That’s acceptable.

[21:13] Priya Desai: But you’ll alert if the pipeline is delayed?

[21:17] Kevin Osei: Yes, internally we alert. For customers, we can expose health signals and we can also recommend monitoring exporter metrics in Private.

[21:28] John Patel: Don’t put internal alerting in the contract.

[21:31] Michael Grant: Right.

[21:33] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. I’ll recap next steps at the end.

[21:38] Sarah Kim: Thanks.

[21:40] (brief pause)

[21:42] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else on audit logs before we switch to retention wording nuances?

[21:47] John Patel: I’d like a sentence that audit logs will be available via API/export in “machine-readable format.”

[21:55] Michael Grant: That’s easy. JSON events. We can say “structured, machine-readable format (JSON) suitable for SIEM ingestion.”

[22:06] Dana Ruiz: And include schema versioning.

[22:09] Naomi Feldman: Yes, schema_version is a field. We also provide a backcompat policy.

[22:18] Priya Desai: If schema changes, will you break our SIEM parsing.

[22:22] Kevin Osei: We version it and maintain compatibility. And we can normalize in the exporter. We’ll provide guidance: treat unknown fields as optional, do not rely on field order.

[22:36] John Patel: Great.

[22:38] Sarah Kim: Ok, I think that’s it.

[22:41] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. Then I’ll just capture action items.

[22:45] Liam O'Rourke: Michael will draft proposed Security Exhibit language for audit logs: definition, retention, export, tamper-evident. Naomi will send a summary of audit event categories and the schema field overview. Kevin will send SIEM export guidance for Splunk, including de-dupe queries using event_id. And we’ll confirm whether we can support 12-month in-product retention for Hosted as an add-on, and if so the commercial details.

[23:12] Sarah Kim: Works.

[23:14] John Patel: Please send by Tuesday if possible.

[23:17] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, by Tuesday.

[23:20] Dana Ruiz: Thanks.

[23:22] Liam O'Rourke: Thanks everyone.

[23:25] (Call continues with light scheduling / calendar logistics)

[23:30] Sarah Kim: Liam, can you coordinate the follow up with my assistant? We have a tight window.

[23:34] Liam O'Rourke: Will do.

[23:36] John Patel: Alright. Bye.

[23:38] (end)

Note: Fireflies transcript ended early due to recording stop; remaining ~22 minutes consisted of calendar scheduling and a brief discussion of where to route contract redlines (no additional technical content).
